educational_summary: An ultra-short-period super-Earth (~1.72× Earth; ~4.1 Earth masses) completing a blistering ~0.605-day orbit at ~0.0118 AU around a cool M-dwarf (~3920 K). With Teq ~1336 K and likely tidal locking, it’s ideal for lessons on the rocky/volatile “radius-valley,” heat redistribution on molten daysides, and how repeated transits enable precise ephemerides for USP terrestrial worlds.

A massive hot Jupiter (~3.35 MJ; ~1.30 RJ) circling an F-type star (~6310 K) every ~4.08 days (Teq ~1728 K). Its high mass, modest inflation, and near-circular orbit make it a textbook case for migration scenarios, secondary-eclipse/phase-curve observations, and comparing irradiation-driven inflation across hot-Jupiter populations.

A warm mini-Neptune (~2.72× Earth; ~9.5 M⊕) with a short ~4.65-day period and notably non-zero eccentricity (e~0.19). Around a K0V host, it’s great for discussing tidal circularization timescales, mass–radius–density inferences, and why eccentric, close-in sub-Neptunes are valuable probes of dynamical histories.

A compact sub-Neptune (~2.34× Earth; ~8.6 M⊕) on a ~3.13-day, near-circular orbit (e≈0) around a K6V star (~4230 K; Teq ~860 K). Sitting near the radius valley with a measured mass, it’s perfect for teaching envelope fractions, photoevaporation/core-powered mass loss, and RV+transit joint characterization.

A hot sub-Neptune (~4.1× Earth; ~25 M⊕) with a ~3.32-day year and high eccentricity (e~0.34). The unusually elliptical, close-in orbit highlights tidal dissipation, circularization pathways, and how eccentricity shapes climate/irradiation cycles on short-period mid-size worlds.

A dense warm mini-Neptune (~3.42× Earth; ~22.4 M⊕) orbiting in ~2.11 days (Teq ~1400 K) with mild eccentricity. Excellent for mass–radius composition modeling (rock/ice core + volatile envelope), and for contrasting scale heights and atmospheric detectability among hot sub-Neptunes.

A temperate sub-Neptune (~2.45× Earth; ~6.6 M⊕) on an ~11.07-day orbit (Teq ~560 K) around a cool K/M-type star (~4570 K). Its size and low irradiation make it a promising case for transmission spectroscopy yield estimates and for illustrating the lower-flux side of the radius-valley landscape.

A long-period warm Jupiter (~0.57 MJ; ~1.26 RJ) found by radial velocities with P~502 days and modest eccentricity (e~0.14). This solar-type system showcases RV phase-coverage challenges, mass–eccentricity correlations for cooler giants, and comparisons to our own Jupiter’s orbital regime.

A USP super-Earth (~1.70× Earth; ~3.8 M⊕) whipping around an M3 star in ~0.669 days (Teq ~1070 K). Likely tidally locked and highly irradiated, it’s a clean example for discussing atmospheric escape limits, dayside–nightside contrasts, and the detectability of frequent, shallow transits around small stars.

A classic hot Jupiter (~0.79 MJ; ~1.09 RJ) orbiting a G1V star every ~2.26 days (Teq ~1715 K). Its size and flux place it among moderately inflated giants, ideal for teaching hot-Jupiter occurrence, migration channels, and secondary-eclipse feasibility around Sun-like hosts.

A short-period (~2.39-day) small planet (~1.39× Earth reported with ~57 M⊕ mass) around an M0V star—values that, if confirmed, imply an unusually high density. In a three-planet system with mild eccentricity (e~0.14), it’s useful for lessons on multi-planet dynamics, mass-radius outliers, and catalog cross-validation.

A warm Jupiter (~0.97 MJ; ~1.00 RJ) on a ~3.71-day orbit around a K-dwarf (~4670 K; Teq ~960 K). Slight eccentricity hints at ongoing tidal evolution, making it a good case for energy dissipation, RV+transit joint fits, and irradiation differences between hot and warm Jupiters.

An inflated Saturn-mass world (~0.21 MJ; ~1.04 RJ) with a ~9.57-day year around an evolved, larger-radius star (~2.0 R☉). The low density and subgiant host enable discussions on stellar evolution changing transit depths, planetary inflation mechanisms, and irradiation histories.

A warm sub-Neptune (~3.28× Earth) with a ~10.36-day orbit in a compact three-planet system around a K-dwarf. Its multi-planet context is ideal for TTV studies, resonance checks, and comparative planetology across siblings receiving similar but distinct irradiation.

A temperate sub-Neptune (~2.47× Earth; ~6.7 M⊕) orbiting an M2 star every ~6.08 days (Teq ~530 K). Around a small, cool host, it’s well-suited for atmospheric follow-up (high transmission signal per scale height) and for illustrating habitability-adjacent regimes around red dwarfs.

A cool, likely rocky super-Earth (~1.33× Earth; ~7.4 M⊕) with a ~28.17-day orbit (Teq ~297 K) around an M2.5V star. Its temperate irradiation and measured mass make it a standout for density/composition lessons, tidal locking expectations, and prospects for atmosphere retention around M dwarfs.

An extreme ultra-hot Jupiter (~5 MJ; ~1.35 RJ) racing around its star in ~0.672 days with dayside temperatures ~3600 K. It’s a benchmark for atmospheric escape, thermal dissociation, and heat-transport physics—perfect for secondary eclipses and phase-curve investigations.

A massive warm Jupiter (~5.3 MJ; ~1.10 RJ) on a ~10.26-day, moderately eccentric orbit (e~0.18) around a slightly evolved F-type star. Great for exploring high-mass giant structure, tidal circularization, and how larger host-star radii influence transit observables.

A hot Jupiter (~2.8 MJ; ~1.28 RJ) with a ~3.38-day orbit (Teq ~1800 K) around a hot, metal-rich star. Its high irradiation and substantial mass make it ideal for emission spectroscopy, albedo constraints, and comparing inflation levels across similarly hot giants.

A cool, eccentric sub-Neptune (~2.19× Earth; ~6 M⊕) with a ~35.19-day period and large e (~0.5) around an M3 star. This system invites discussions of seasonal forcing on eccentric temperate worlds, transmission-spectroscopy metrics (TSM) for small cool hosts, and dynamical excitation.

A highly eccentric warm Jupiter (~6 MJ; ~1.0 RJ) with P~22.65 days and e≈0.68 around a Sun-like star. Its extreme periastron passages are perfect for teaching high-e migration (e.g., Kozai–Lidov), tidal circularization, and periastron heating signatures.

A warm sub-Neptune (~2.75× Earth; ~8.0 M⊕) on a ~7.99-day orbit (Teq ~1020 K) around a Sun-like star. With both mass and radius measured, it’s useful for density-driven interior modeling, atmospheric scale-height estimates, and the volatile-retention frontier.

An extremely inflated hot-Saturn (~0.61 MJ; ~1.76 RJ) with a ~6.20-day period around an evolved star (~4.1 R☉). It’s a showcase for irradiation-driven inflation, stellar evolution effects on close-in giants, and the challenges of measuring low densities precisely.

A hot Saturn (~0.37 MJ; ~1.15 RJ) orbiting every ~3.55 days (Teq ~1470 K) around a slightly metal-rich G-type star. The combination of modest mass and inflated radius makes it a prime example for comparing inflation mechanisms and atmospheric detectability versus gravity.

A typical hot Jupiter (~1.7 MJ; ~1.17 RJ) with a short ~2.35-day, circular orbit (Teq ~1540 K) around a G-type star. Its clean geometry and strong irradiation are well suited for phase curves, secondary eclipses, and migration-history discussions.

A warm Neptune (~5.14× Earth; ~15 M⊕) on a ~4.67-day orbit around an M2V star (~3580 K; Teq ~580 K). Around a small host, it’s compelling for transmission spectroscopy forecasts and for exploring how sub-Neptunes around M dwarfs differ from those around Sun-like stars.

A hot Jupiter (~1.11 MJ; ~1.17 RJ) with a ~3.24-day, circular orbit (Teq ~1630 K) around a slightly metal-rich star. It’s a solid case for irradiation/inflation comparisons, equilibrium-temperature calculations, and joint RV–transit characterization.

A rare, massive warm Jupiter (~2.48 MJ; ~1.22 RJ) orbiting an M-dwarf (~3790 K) every ~3.58 days (Teq ~725 K). Its metal-rich host ([Fe/H]~+0.52) and high planet mass enable lessons on giant-planet occurrence versus metallicity and why such heavy giants around M stars are uncommon.

A warm sub-Neptune (~2.42× Earth; ~6.4 M⊕) with a ~9.15-day period (Teq ~760 K). With both mass and radius measured around a Sun-like/K-type host, it’s excellent for density/composition inference, atmospheric loss thresholds, and RV–transit synergies.

An ultra-short-period sub-Neptune (~2.8× Earth; mass poorly constrained) orbiting an M3 star in ~1.16 days. Its intense irradiation and small host produce deep, frequent transits—great for illustrating USP demographics just above the rocky cutoff and the role of host type in detectability.
